name: Tart cherry juice

lead: Tart cherry juice comes from sour cherries, most often the Montmorency cultivar, sold as juice or concentrate. People drink it for exercise recovery and as a food source of melatonin before bed, aiming for less soreness, more training and a more rested appearance.

Proponents point to melatonin and anthocyanin antioxidants. A randomized crossover study of 20 volunteers examined whether a concentrate raised urinary melatonin and improved sleep, a pilot study looked at older adults with insomnia, and other trials measured muscle damage and soreness. Studies are small.

paras: It is drunk as juice or mixed from concentrate, usually in the evening or around hard training, as part of a recovery routine. Users judge it over days to weeks.
It is a food product with sugar content. The sources reviewed give little data on adverse effects.

angle.text: Users drink tart cherry juice for exercise recovery and as a melatonin source for sleep, supporting training and a rested look. Small trials have measured sleep, soreness and muscle-damage markers; appearance effects have not been studied.

lead: Tart cherry juice is juice from sour cherries (Prunus cerasus), most commonly the Montmorency cultivar, grown largely in Michigan [1]. It is drunk or taken as concentrate for exercise recovery and sleep, and appears in recovery and sleep routines in appearance communities.

Interest in it for sleep rests on the claim that tart cherries contain melatonin. A randomized crossover study of 20 volunteers examined whether a tart cherry juice concentrate raised urinary melatonin and improved sleep [2], and a pilot study examined the juice in older adults with insomnia [3]. Other trials examined exercise-induced muscle damage and soreness [4][5][6].

paras: The juice is tart and red from anthocyanin pigments, and is sold as juice, concentrate and capsules [1]. Its prominence rose in the early 2000s after studies on cherries and inflammation and exercise recovery [1].

Sleep: a 2012 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study in 20 volunteers tested a concentrate on urinary melatonin and sleep quality [2]; a 2010 pilot study examined older adults with insomnia [3]; a further pilot in older adults with insomnia (20 participants) was registered in 2025 [7]. A 2016 review surveyed diet and sleep research [8].

Exercise recovery: a study of 20 recreational marathon runners tested juice before and after a marathon on markers of muscle damage, inflammation and oxidative stress [4]; a 2006 crossover trial in 14 male students tested a cherry juice blend against exercise-induced muscle damage [5]; a randomized trial examined muscle pain during running [6].

Other registered studies cover oxidative stress, uric acid, cardiovascular risk and chemotherapy-related neuropathy [9][10]. The effect sizes and conclusions of these studies were not reviewed in detail.
The juice contains sugar, and the product is generally sold as a food. Specific adverse-effect data were not available in the sources reviewed.

timeline.event: Trial of a tart cherry juice blend on exercise-induced muscle damage [5].
